title: Software Extensions: IDE Extensions
summary: Integrated development environment extensions are plugins that add features to a code editor or full development suite, and they deserve their own entry because the host grants them a different and in some ways richer level of access than a browser does. An extension declared to run at editor start executes each time the developer opens the tool, and it usually runs with the permissions of the developer account, which in many organisations means access to source code repositories, package registries, build systems and cloud credentials held in the developer workspace. The installation paths mirror the parent technique: a malicious or typosquatted listing in the extension marketplace, a legitimate extension that is sold or compromised and then updated, or a direct side load in which the extension is copied into the editor extension folder on disk. A distinguishing feature of this sub-technique is that the extension can also be benign and still serve the attacker, because editors now offer remote development and port forwarding features that can create a durable tunnel from the developer machine into other networks. Detection work therefore covers three surfaces: the extension folder inside the user profile and the metadata files that record installed plugins, the editor process itself as a parent of unexpected shells or network clients, and outbound connections to addresses that the organisation does not associate with package downloads or source control. Comparing the installed extension list against a team baseline is the practical control, and it also catches extensions that were side loaded and never passed through a marketplace review.

beginner.definition: An IDE extension is an add-on for the program a developer uses to write code. Examples include code checkers and tools that talk to Git or Docker. This technique is when an attacker uses such an add-on to stay on a developer machine.
beginner.whyItMatters: Developer machines hold source code, tokens and access to build systems. An extension runs every time the editor opens and can use all of that. It can also open a tunnel out of the network, which is especially useful to an attacker. One install can give away a whole product.
howItWorks: Code editors load extensions from a hidden folder inside the developer profile.
An extension can be set to run as soon as the editor opens.
An attacker publishes a fake extension or side loads one directly onto disk.
The extension then runs again every single time the developer starts the editor.
It can read source code, steal tokens or start a hidden network tunnel.
Because the editor is trusted, this traffic often looks normal to the network.
beginner.example: Think of a contractor given an office key so they can work at a desk. The key also opens the room where every project file is kept. The contractor comes in every morning, works normally, and each night copies one page of every plan into a bag by the door.
takeaways: Developer tools are high value targets because they hold code and credentials.
An extension can be installed by copying files and never appear in a store.
Watch the editor process for child shells and unusual outbound connections.

objectives: Explain what an IDE extension is and when it executes.
Describe how this sub-technique differs from the parent technique Software Extensions.
Compare the risk of an IDE extension with the risk of a browser extension.
Identify the extension directories and metadata that reveal an installed plugin.
Explain how a benign remote development extension can be abused as a tunnel.
